rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods / Results; the authors ran their own 10-week laboratory anticlogging tests (two circulating platforms, 10 laterals, 2% urea vs. control) and measured emitter discharge, dry weight of clogging materials, microbial counts, XRD/SEM of clogging materials and urea adsorption kinetics.
rows.notes: The study is a laboratory emitter-clogging experiment with muddy water and urea fertigation; no crop was grown and no yield, crop quality or nutrient-consumption outcome was measured, nor any comparison of an 'advanced' drip system against a conventional one. What it shows is that urea muddy-water fertigation does not accelerate clogging in the first 35 days but increases dry weight of clogging materials and discharge reduction afterwards (Figs 4-5, Table 5), with actinomycete growth and CaCO3 precipitation proposed as mechanisms. It provides no evidence on the crop-production effect claimed in the passage.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods / Results; own laboratory anticlogging experiment (10 cycles, May-July 2016) with measured emitter discharge, clogging-material dry weight, microbial counts, XRD and SEM data.
rows.notes: The study contains nothing on pesticide applications, pests, diseases or crops. Its only biological results concern bacteria, fungi and actinomycete counts in lateral sediments inside the drip laterals (Table 4) as they relate to emitter clogging, not to crop pest control. It therefore offers no evidence for the claim that drip/ADI reduces pesticide applications compared with conventional drip.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a laboratory study of emitter clogging under urea fertigation with Yellow-River-type muddy water; it is being cited by the review for agronomic claims (yield, quality, pesticide reduction) that it does not address.
